Get started with zutable

Source: vignettes/zutable.Rmd
zutable.Rmd
library(zutable)

A data.frame does not know its types: a column can change from integer to character with one assignment, and the error surfaces only when the data reaches the code that breaks. A zutable always knows its schema, and every query is checked against it before any data is read. This page builds one small table of trades and takes it through a query, a type error, a join, an update and its plan. How the joins behave, and how fast the kernel underneath is, are left to the articles.

A table with a schema

zutable() builds a table from columns, as data.frame() does, and gives each column a logical type. schema() shows them: the name, the type, and whether the column may hold missing values.

trades <- zutable(
  id       = c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L),
  day      = as.Date("2026-01-01") + 0:4,
  px       = c(10.5, 11, 20, 19.5, 7),
  qty      = c(100L, 50L, 10L, 30L, 200L),
  notional = NA_real_
)
schema(trades)
#> <zutable_schema> 5 fields
#>   id int32
#>   day date
#>   px float64
#>   qty int32
#>   notional float64

Query with SQL’s clauses

The bracket takes SQL’s clauses as named arguments over bare column names: where, select, by, having, order, limit and distinct. They run in SQL’s logical order, whatever order they are written in. Here the filter drops the first day before the volume-weighted price is computed per id. .() lists the output columns, and count() and desc() are two of the bracket’s functions, listed in ?vocabulary. The string "2026-01-02" is compared with a date column, so it is read as an ISO 8601 date; a string that is not one is a type error.

trades[where  = day >= "2026-01-02",
       select = .(vwap = sum(px * qty) / sum(qty), n = count()),
       by     = id,
       order  = desc(vwap)]
#> <zutable> 3 rows x 3 columns
#>   id      vwap      n
#>   <int32> <float64> <not_null(int32)>
#> 1 2       19.625    2
#> 2 1       11.000    1
#> 3 3       7.000     1

The result is a zutable too, with a type for every column. n is not_null(int32): a count is never missing, and the schema says so.

Schemas are known before data is

Every function in the bracket comes from a closed, typed vocabulary, so a result’s schema follows from its input’s. Asking for the schema of a query tells you what it will return.

schema(trades[select = .(.all, value = px * qty)])
#> <zutable_schema> 6 fields
#>   id int32
#>   day date
#>   px float64
#>   qty int32
#>   notional float64
#>   value float64

A value that would change a column’s type is an error, not a silent conversion. qty is an integer column, and px * 2 is a double.

trades[, { qty := px * 2 }]
#> Error in `[.zutable`:
#> ! column `qty` is int32; the update would make it float64

The error has the class zutable_schema_error, so code can catch it without matching its message.

Join another table

join() matches rows on key columns, as an inner join unless how says otherwise. The pairs come in x’s row order, and a key that matches several rows of y gives every pair unless multiple asks for the first, the last, or an error.

firms <- zutable(id = c(1L, 2L, 4L), name = c("Acme", "Globex", "Initech"))
join(trades, firms, on = id)
#> <zutable> 4 rows x 6 columns
#>   id      day        px        qty     notional  name
#>   <int32> <date>     <float64> <int32> <float64> <string>
#> 1 1       2026-01-01 10.5      100     NA        Acme
#> 2 1       2026-01-02 11.0      50      NA        Acme
#> 3 2       2026-01-03 20.0      10      NA        Globex
#> 4 2       2026-01-04 19.5      30      NA        Globex
join(trades, firms, on = id, how = "left")
#> <zutable> 5 rows x 6 columns
#>   id      day        px        qty     notional  name
#>   <int32> <date>     <float64> <int32> <float64> <string>
#> 1 1       2026-01-01 10.5      100     NA        Acme
#> 2 1       2026-01-02 11.0      50      NA        Acme
#> 3 2       2026-01-03 20.0      10      NA        Globex
#> 4 2       2026-01-04 19.5      30      NA        Globex
#> 5 3       2026-01-05 7.0       200     NA        NA

The inner join drops id 3, which has no firm; the left join keeps it with a missing name.

Update in place, then freeze

:= writes into existing columns in place, and never adds one. A block of updates is checked as a whole before anything is written. freeze() marks the point where a table’s values are final; a later update is an error.

trades[, {
  notional := px * qty
}]
#> <zutable> 5 rows x 5 columns
#>   id      day        px        qty     notional
#>   <int32> <date>     <float64> <int32> <float64>
#> 1 1       2026-01-01 10.5      100     1050
#> 2 1       2026-01-02 11.0      50      550
#> 3 2       2026-01-03 20.0      10      200
#> 4 2       2026-01-04 19.5      30      585
#> 5 3       2026-01-05 7.0       200     1400
freeze(trades)
trades
#> <zutable> 5 rows x 5 columns, frozen
#>   id      day        px        qty     notional
#>   <int32> <date>     <float64> <int32> <float64>
#> 1 1       2026-01-01 10.5      100     1050
#> 2 1       2026-01-02 11.0      50      550
#> 3 2       2026-01-03 20.0      10      200
#> 4 2       2026-01-04 19.5      30      585
#> 5 3       2026-01-05 7.0       200     1400

See how a table was made

Each table keeps the plan that made it. explain() prints it one step per line: the source with its schema, the update made earlier, then the filter of this query. The plan is a record of how the values came to be; printing it runs nothing.

big <- trades[where = qty > 20L]
explain(big)
#> source  <anonymous table>  id int32, day date, px float64, qty int32, notional float64
#> update  notional := (px * qty)
#> filter  (qty > 20L)
